The shared pathways include genes that control GABA, a brain chemical that helps calm nerve signals, and also genes that control how neurons use signals and receptors. The similarity scores show how often the two conditions have the same symptoms. The score is 0.18 with the Lubs type disorder (fairly close) and 0.10 with the encephalopathy (less similar).

Rett Syndrome also shares two pathways with Witteveen‑Kolk syndrome, and one pathway with a disorder that causes hand movements and language problems. The scores for these links are 0.08, which means the similarities are weaker. No other conditions in the atlas are shown to have a strong shared pathway with Rett Syndrome.

There are conditions that look like Rett Syndrome by how they make people feel (the same symptoms), such as the disease with hyper‑motile movements and seizures or the one with an early brain loss. However, the atlas finds no shared biological pathways for these conditions, so it isn’t clear if they work in the same way as Rett Syndrome.

Trofinetide (Daybue) is the only drug listed in the atlas for Rett Syndrome; it has been proven to work in clinical studies. It is a synthetic cousin of a small piece of the insulin‑like growth factor 1 protein, but how it helps is still not fully understood.

The atlas also notes that the Rett condition is caused by changes in the MECP2 gene on the X chromosome, and that people with Rett Syndrome often have trouble with their nervous system and can develop a wide‑based walking pattern. These features come from scientific papers that have studied the gene and the symptoms.
